title: Expanded A1–C2 Curriculum
description: Adds Units 5–10 to every course stage while preserving all original lesson IDs and progress.

lessons.title: Food and Cafés: Core language
lessons.subtitle: Grammar, vocabulary and controlled practice

grammar.title: Countable and uncountable nouns
grammar.rule: Use a/an with one countable noun, plural forms with countable nouns, and some/any with quantities. Use much with uncountable nouns and many with plural countable nouns.
examples: I would like a sandwich.
We need some water.
Are there any apples?

vocab.definition: food eaten at a regular time
vocab.example: The unit uses “meal” while discussing meals, quantities and ordering politely.

vocab.definition: a list of food and drinks available
vocab.example: The unit uses “menu” while discussing meals, quantities and ordering politely.

vocab.definition: ask for food or drink in a café or restaurant
vocab.example: The unit uses “order” while discussing meals, quantities and ordering politely.

vocab.definition: one of the foods used to make a dish
vocab.example: The unit uses “ingredient” while discussing meals, quantities and ordering politely.

vocab.definition: needing or wanting food
vocab.example: The unit uses “hungry” while discussing meals, quantities and ordering politely.

vocab.definition: a statement showing how much must be paid
vocab.example: The unit uses “bill” while discussing meals, quantities and ordering politely.

phrasal.definition: eat in a restaurant or café
phrasal.example: Use “eat out” naturally when discussing meals, quantities and ordering politely.

phrasal.definition: say that you would like to receive something
phrasal.example: Use “ask for” naturally when discussing meals, quantities and ordering politely.

lessons.reading: Rami meets a friend at a small café. He orders a cheese sandwich and some orange juice. His friend asks for soup, but there is not any soup left. The waiter recommends a salad instead. At the end, they ask for the bill and pay together.
lessons.listening: Good afternoon. Are you ready to order? Yes, please. I would like a chicken sandwich and some tea. Do you have any fruit? We have apples and bananas today.
lessons.speaking: Role-play ordering a meal. Greet the server, ask about one item, order food and drink, and ask for the bill.
lessons.writing: Write a simple café order or a short description of a meal you enjoy.
lessons.homework: Make a shopping list for three meals. Mark countable and uncountable nouns.

units.title: Shopping and Prices
units.theme: clothes, prices, sizes and simple choices

lessons.title: Shopping and Prices: Core language
lessons.subtitle: Grammar, vocabulary and controlled practice

grammar.title: This, that, these and those
grammar.rule: Use this/these for things near you and that/those for things farther away. Use how much to ask about price.
examples: How much is this shirt?
Those shoes are too large.
These trousers are comfortable.

vocab.definition: the amount of money needed to buy something
vocab.example: The unit uses “price” while discussing clothes, prices, sizes and simple choices.

vocab.definition: a measurement showing how large or small something is
vocab.example: The unit uses “size” while discussing clothes, prices, sizes and simple choices.

vocab.definition: money in coins or notes
vocab.example: The unit uses “cash” while discussing clothes, prices, sizes and simple choices.

vocab.definition: money returned after paying more than the price
vocab.example: The unit uses “change” while discussing clothes, prices, sizes and simple choices.

vocab.definition: costing little money
vocab.example: The unit uses “cheap” while discussing clothes, prices, sizes and simple choices.

vocab.definition: costing a lot of money
vocab.example: The unit uses “expensive” while discussing clothes, prices, sizes and simple choices.

phrasal.definition: put on clothes to check their size or appearance
phrasal.example: Use “try on” naturally when discussing clothes, prices, sizes and simple choices.

phrasal.definition: give money in exchange for something
phrasal.example: Use “pay for” naturally when discussing clothes, prices, sizes and simple choices.

lessons.reading: Sara needs a jacket for work. She tries on a black jacket, but it is too small. A blue one fits well and is cheaper. She asks the assistant how much it costs, pays by card and keeps the receipt.
lessons.listening: Can I help you? Yes, I am looking for a medium shirt. How much is this one? It is twenty-five dollars. You can try it on over there.
lessons.speaking: Describe two items in a shop and choose one. Mention colour, size, price and comfort.
lessons.writing: Write a short message about something you bought. Include the price and why you chose it.
lessons.homework: Compare five items at home using this, that, these and those.

grammar.title: Future forms
grammar.rule: Use will for predictions and immediate decisions, going to for intentions or evidence-based predictions, and present continuous for arrangements.
examples: I think demand will increase.
We are going to redesign the course.
I am meeting the trainer on Monday.

vocab.definition: a result that someone intends to achieve
vocab.example: The unit uses “goal” while discussing plans, predictions and scheduled events.

vocab.definition: a specific level or result to aim for
vocab.example: The unit uses “target” while discussing plans, predictions and scheduled events.

vocab.definition: a statement about what is expected to happen
vocab.example: The unit uses “forecast” while discussing plans, predictions and scheduled events.

vocab.definition: a plan agreed with other people
vocab.example: The unit uses “arrangement” while discussing plans, predictions and scheduled events.

vocab.definition: something that a person plans to do
vocab.example: The unit uses “intention” while discussing plans, predictions and scheduled events.

vocab.definition: an important stage in progress
vocab.example: The unit uses “milestone” while discussing plans, predictions and scheduled events.

phrasal.definition: prepare for future needs or events
phrasal.example: Use “plan ahead” naturally when discussing plans, predictions and scheduled events.

phrasal.definition: try to achieve a particular result
phrasal.example: Use “aim for” naturally when discussing plans, predictions and scheduled events.

lessons.reading: A small company is planning ahead for the next year. It is going to introduce online appointments, and managers predict that customer waiting times will fall. The technical team is meeting a software provider next week to confirm the schedule.
lessons.listening: We are presenting the proposal on Thursday. I think the directors will ask about cost, so I am going to prepare a clearer budget slide.

units.title: Global Challenges
units.theme: complex issues, institutions and connected causes

lessons.title: Global Challenges: Core language
lessons.subtitle: Grammar, vocabulary and controlled practice

grammar.title: Complex noun phrases
grammar.rule: Build precise noun phrases with premodification, postmodification and relative or prepositional detail, while avoiding unnecessary density.
examples: long-term regional water-management agreements
communities affected by repeated coastal flooding
the rapid expansion of low-cost renewable-energy capacity

vocab.definition: a relationship in which people or systems depend on one another
vocab.example: The unit uses “interdependence” while discussing complex issues, institutions and connected causes.

vocab.definition: basic systems and structures needed for society to function
vocab.example: The unit uses “infrastructure” while discussing complex issues, institutions and connected causes.

vocab.definition: an unfair difference in resources or opportunities
vocab.example: The unit uses “inequality” while discussing complex issues, institutions and connected causes.

vocab.definition: movement of people from one place to another
vocab.example: The unit uses “migration” while discussing complex issues, institutions and connected causes.

vocab.definition: change made to manage new conditions
vocab.example: The unit uses “adaptation” while discussing complex issues, institutions and connected causes.

vocab.definition: joint action toward a shared purpose
vocab.example: The unit uses “cooperation” while discussing complex issues, institutions and connected causes.

phrasal.definition: take action because of a situation
phrasal.example: Use “respond to” naturally when discussing complex issues, institutions and connected causes.

phrasal.definition: need someone or something for support or success
phrasal.example: Use “depend on” naturally when discussing complex issues, institutions and connected causes.

lessons.reading: Regional climate adaptation depends on more than isolated local projects. Communities affected by repeated flooding need reliable early-warning infrastructure, long-term financing and agreements that recognise cross-border interdependence. Without cooperation, one area’s protective measures may transfer risk elsewhere.
lessons.listening: The rapid growth of urban populations is creating pressure on transport, housing and water systems. Effective responses depend on coordinated planning rather than separate short-term projects.
lessons.speaking: Explain a global challenge by identifying connected causes, affected groups and possible responses.
lessons.writing: Write a structured overview using clear but information-rich noun phrases.
lessons.homework: Edit five overly dense noun phrases for clarity and five vague phrases for precision.

grammar.title: Wish, if only and mixed conditionals
grammar.rule: Use wish/if only plus past perfect for regret about the past, and mixed conditionals when an unreal past affects the present.
examples: I wish we had tested the system earlier.
If only the warning had been clearer.
If we had invested then, we would be better prepared now.

vocab.definition: a possible future event that must be prepared for
vocab.example: The unit uses “contingency” while discussing unreal past alternatives and present consequences.

vocab.definition: a mistake caused by failing to notice something
vocab.example: The unit uses “oversight” while discussing unreal past alternatives and present consequences.

vocab.definition: the degree to which someone or something is at risk
vocab.example: The unit uses “exposure” while discussing unreal past alternatives and present consequences.

vocab.definition: action taken to reduce harmful effects
vocab.example: The unit uses “mitigation” while discussing unreal past alternatives and present consequences.

vocab.definition: an idea accepted without complete proof
vocab.example: The unit uses “assumption” while discussing unreal past alternatives and present consequences.

vocab.definition: a possible sequence of future events
vocab.example: The unit uses “scenario” while discussing unreal past alternatives and present consequences.

phrasal.definition: prepare for a possible event
phrasal.example: Use “plan for” naturally when discussing unreal past alternatives and present consequences.

phrasal.definition: fail to notice or consider something
phrasal.example: Use “overlook” naturally when discussing unreal past alternatives and present consequences.

grammar.rule: Use roughly, approximately, just over, nearly, a minority, a substantial proportion and similar expressions to describe data precisely without false accuracy.
examples: Just over half of respondents supported the change.

A small minority reported no improvement.

lessons.title: Policy and Governance: Core language
lessons.subtitle: Grammar, vocabulary and controlled practice

grammar.title: Advanced passive and agency
grammar.rule: Use passive structures to manage focus, but name the agent when responsibility is important. Avoid passives that obscure accountability.
examples: The decision was approved after consultation.
The records are believed to have been altered.
Senior management authorised the change.

vocab.definition: the system by which an organisation or society is directed and controlled
vocab.example: The unit uses “governance” while discussing authority, accountability and institutional decisions.

vocab.definition: official authority or instruction to act
vocab.example: The unit uses “mandate” while discussing authority, accountability and institutional decisions.

vocab.definition: supervision intended to ensure correct conduct
vocab.example: The unit uses “oversight” while discussing authority, accountability and institutional decisions.

vocab.definition: the quality of being accepted as lawful or justified
vocab.example: The unit uses “legitimacy” while discussing authority, accountability and institutional decisions.

vocab.definition: the transfer of responsibility or authority
vocab.example: The unit uses “delegation” while discussing authority, accountability and institutional decisions.

vocab.definition: the obligation to explain and accept responsibility for actions
vocab.example: The unit uses “accountability” while discussing authority, accountability and institutional decisions.

phrasal.definition: be responsible to a person or authority
phrasal.example: Use “answer to” naturally when discussing authority, accountability and institutional decisions.

phrasal.definition: give formal approval to a decision or document

lessons.reading: Organisations often state one set of values and reward another. Staff may buy into an official message initially, but repeated decisions reveal which norms genuinely matter. lessons.speaking: Analyse the difference between stated values and actual organisational behaviour.
lessons.writing: Write a cultural diagnosis using concise reference, substitution and evidence.
lessons.homework: Identify three visible or invisible cultural signals in an organisation.

grammar.title: Future in the past and prospective language
grammar.rule: Use was/were going to, would, was/were due to and was/were expected to when describing a future viewed from a past point. Use prospective language to distinguish forecasts from scenarios.
examples: The technology was expected to reduce cost.
The pilot was due to begin in March.
Analysts believed the market would change rapidly.

lessons.reading: A technically accurate presentation can still fail if the audience cannot see its structure. Effective speakers signal where they are, why a point matters and how it connects to the recommendation. They also adapt detail, pace and examples to the decisions the audience must make.
lessons.listening: Let me sum up the evidence before moving on to the recommendation. The central point is not that risk can be removed; it is that exposure can be reduced at a reasonable cost.

lessons.homework: Record two versions of the opening and evaluate clarity, pace and emphasis.

lessons.reading: A subsidy increased access to a service, but it also fed into higher demand before capacity expanded. grammar.title: Punctuation and sentence architecture
grammar.rule: Use colons, semicolons, dashes, parentheses and sentence boundaries to clarify relationships and control rhythm, not merely to decorate prose.
examples: The evidence supports one conclusion: implementation failed.
The plan was ambitious; the timetable was not credible.
One risk—the loss of specialist staff—received little attention.

vocab.definition: the underlying structure of a text or system
vocab.example: The unit uses “architecture” while discussing sentence design, punctuation and paragraph movement.

vocab.definition: the linguistic connection between parts of a text
vocab.example: The unit uses “cohesion” while discussing sentence design, punctuation and paragraph movement.

vocab.definition: the rhythm produced by sentence length and stress
vocab.example: The unit uses “cadence” while discussing sentence design, punctuation and paragraph movement.

vocab.definition: a temporary movement away from the main subject
vocab.example: The unit uses “digression” while discussing sentence design, punctuation and paragraph movement.

vocab.definition: repetition of grammatical structure for clarity or effect
vocab.example: The unit uses “parallelism” while discussing sentence design, punctuation and paragraph movement.

vocab.definition: special attention or importance given to an idea
vocab.example: The unit uses “emphasis” while discussing sentence design, punctuation and paragraph movement.

phrasal.definition: divide something into smaller sections
phrasal.example: Use “break up” naturally when discussing sentence design, punctuation and paragraph movement.

phrasal.definition: connect a later point to an earlier central idea
phrasal.example: Use “tie back to” naturally when discussing sentence design, punctuation and paragraph movement.

lessons.reading: Long sentences are not inherently sophisticated, nor are short ones automatically clear. lessons.homework: Produce three stylistically different versions of the same paragraph and explain the effects.

grammar.title: Lexicogrammatical precision
grammar.rule: At proficiency level, choices are judged not only for correctness but also for connotation, collocation, register and implied agency.
examples: The policy triggered concern, whereas the announcement merely prompted questions.
The evidence is sparse, not necessarily weak.

vocab.definition: a combination of words that commonly occur together

vocab.definition: a style of language appropriate to a context
vocab.example: The unit uses “register” while discussing connotation, collocation and exact lexical choice.

vocab.definition: the level of detail at which information is described
vocab.example: The unit uses “granularity” while discussing connotation, collocation and exact lexical choice.

vocab.definition: the condition of having the same meaning, value or effect

grammar.title: Advanced pragmatics
grammar.rule: Interpretation depends on literal wording, tone, shared knowledge, power relationships and whether a remark protects or threatens social face.
examples: ‘Excellent timing’ may express praise or criticism depending on context.
Understatement can intensify rather than weaken criticism.
A joke that builds solidarity in one group may exclude another.

vocab.definition: humour that criticises people, institutions or ideas
vocab.example: The unit uses “satire” while discussing playful language, face and context.

vocab.definition: presentation of something as less serious than it is
vocab.example: The unit uses “understatement” while discussing playful language, face and context.

vocab.definition: mocking language that often means the opposite of its words
vocab.example: The unit uses “sarcasm” while discussing playful language, face and context.

vocab.definition: a comfortable and trusting relationship
vocab.example: The unit uses “rapport” while discussing playful language, face and context.

vocab.definition: a person’s public social dignity or self-image
vocab.example: The unit uses “face” while discussing playful language, face and context.

vocab.definition: a mismatch that creates surprise or humour
vocab.example: The unit uses “incongruity” while discussing playful language, face and context.

phrasal.definition: use the contrast or relationship between things for effect
phrasal.example: Use “play off” naturally when discussing playful language, face and context.

phrasal.definition: produce the intended positive response
phrasal.example: Use “land well” naturally when discussing playful language, face and context.

lessons.reading: Humour often depends on an incongruity that listeners recognise together. Yet the same joke may not land well across differences in language, status or experience. Sarcasm can strengthen rapport among close colleagues but threaten face when trust is uncertain.

lessons.speaking: Interpret humour or irony in a professional or social exchange and discuss alternative readings.
lessons.writing: Analyse how a humorous passage creates effect and where misunderstanding could arise.
lessons.homework: Collect five examples of irony or understatement and annotate the contextual clues.

lessons.reading: Editorial mastery involves deciding what a text is trying to do before correcting how each sentence is written. A polished paragraph can still damage coherence if it interrupts the argument. Strong editing foregrounds the reader’s questions, preserves necessary terminology and cuts away material that competes with the main purpose.

grammar.title: Rhetorical control under challenge
grammar.rule: Combine framing, concession, evidence, rebuttal and audience awareness without misrepresenting uncertainty or opposing views.
examples: The objection identifies a real cost; it does not, however, invalidate the need for action.
Our case rests not on certainty but on the asymmetry of the risk.
To reject the proposal, one would need to show that the alternative is both safer and feasible.

vocab.definition: public support for a cause, policy or group

vocab.definition: a reasoned response showing an argument is incomplete or mistaken

vocab.definition: presentation that influences how an issue is understood
vocab.example: The unit uses “framing” while discussing ethical persuasion, public reasoning and opposition.

vocab.definition: the responsibility to provide evidence for a claim
vocab.example: The unit uses “burden of proof” while discussing ethical persuasion, public reasoning and opposition.

vocab.definition: the relationship between the seriousness of a problem and the response
vocab.example: The unit uses “proportionality” while discussing ethical persuasion, public reasoning and opposition.

vocab.definition: accepted justification or rightful authority
vocab.example: The unit uses “legitimacy” while discussing ethical persuasion, public reasoning and opposition.

phrasal.definition: present reasons supporting an action or belief
phrasal.example: Use “make the case for” naturally when discussing ethical persuasion, public reasoning and opposition.

phrasal.definition: resist or challenge an argument or pressure
phrasal.example: Use “push back against” naturally when discussing ethical persuasion, public reasoning and opposition.
